summary: This informational document sets out basic requirements for an IPv6 Customer Edge router, the home or small-office box that connects a site to its provider. It focuses on how the router gets its own IPv6 setup and how it provisions the hosts behind it. It was replaced by RFC 7084.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a checklist for the box in your home that connects you to the internet, saying how it should handle IPv6 for itself and your devices. It was later replaced by RFC 7084.

questions: what is a customer edge router
how does ipv6 work in my home
subtitle: Requirements for home and small-office routers to support IPv6.

tldr.problem: Home and small-office routers need clear requirements for supporting IPv6 configuration, both obtaining IPv6 connectivity from the service provider and distributing it to local devices.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies detailed requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge routers covering how they obtain and manage IPv6 addresses on the WAN side, how they provision IPv6 on the LAN side using Neighbor Discovery and DHCPv6, and how they implement basic security filters.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 deployment in residential and small-office networks became more consistent and interoperable. This was superseded by RFC 7084.

today: RFC 6204 is obsoleted by RFC 7084, which provides updated requirements for IPv6 customer edge routers reflecting changes in IPv6 deployment and technology since 2011.

sections.title: IPv6 Customer Edge Router Basics
sections.content:
An IPv6 Customer Edge (CE) router is the device at the boundary between a home or small office network and the service provider network. It typically sits between the internet connection and the devices in the house or office, forwards IPv6 packets, and helps local devices acquire IPv6 addresses and configuration.

This document specifies what an IPv6 CE router must and should do. Most home routers today support both IPv4 and IPv6. The document focuses on automatic provisioning of a single router with multiple LAN interfaces; complex multi-router topologies are out of scope. The router must obtain IPv6 connectivity from the service provider through its WAN interface and then distribute that connectivity to hosts on its LAN interfaces.

The architecture assumes IPv6 works similarly to how IPv4 does in home networks, but with important differences: IPv6 uses automatic address configuration and prefix delegation rather than NAT, and addresses are more stable and longer-lived.
sections.plainLanguage: The router is the box that connects your home to the internet. It gets IPv6 from your internet company and gives it to your devices. This memo says what it has to do.

sections.title: WAN-Side Configuration: Connecting to the Provider
sections.content:
When the IPv6 CE router connects to the service provider network on its WAN interface, it must perform several automatic provisioning steps:

IPv6 Address Acquisition: The router acts as an IPv6 host on the WAN link. It must generate a link-local address and complete address validation before sending Router Solicitations. It uses Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) to discover the service provider's routers and learn default routes. It should support both Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) and DHCPv6 for getting its own global address.

Prefix Delegation: The router must act as a DHCPv6 requesting router to obtain delegated prefixes from the provider via prefix delegation (RFC 3633). The provider typically gives the router a larger block of addresses (e.g., a /48 or /56 prefix) which the router can subdivide for its LAN networks. The router must be prepared to accept a prefix different from what it requested and should log an error if the prefix is too small.

Link-Layer Support: The router must support IPv6 over common link technologies including Ethernet, PPP, and Data Over Cable specifications. For PPP connections, IPv6 Control Protocol and IPv4 Control Protocol must operate independently.

Default Behavior: By default, the router must not advertise itself as a default router on its LAN side if it has no working IPv6 connectivity on the WAN side. This prevents hosts from trying to use the router as a gateway when it has no internet connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The router connects to your ISP and asks for IPv6 addresses for itself and for all your local devices. It might get a big block of addresses to share with your home network.

sections.title: LAN-Side Configuration: Provisioning Local Devices
sections.content:
Once the IPv6 CE router has obtained IPv6 connectivity on the WAN side, it must help local devices acquire IPv6 addresses and configuration on the LAN side:

Prefix Distribution: The router must assign a separate /64 subnet from its delegated prefixes to each LAN interface. It advertises these prefixes to local devices using Router Advertisements according to RFC 4861. The router must support one or more of these mechanisms: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) where devices auto-generate their own addresses from the advertised prefix, or DHCPv6 where the router acts as a DHCP server assigning addresses to devices.

Unique Local Addresses (ULAs): For communication within the local network that does not require global routing, the router should support Unique Local Addresses (ULAs). These are like private addresses in IPv4. The router should generate a ULA prefix, maintain it consistently across reboots, and allow users to configure it. The router must filter ULA traffic so it does not leak to the WAN side.

DNS and Other Configuration: The router must support DHCPv6 options for providing DNS servers and domain search lists to local devices. It should pass through DNS configuration received from the service provider to local devices.

Prefix Changes: When the delegated prefix changes, the router must immediately advertise the old prefix with zero lifetime to force devices to stop using it, then advertise the new prefix. This allows graceful migration when the provider changes the address allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: The router tells each device in your home what IPv6 address to use, and where to find the internet's DNS servers. It makes sure devices don't try to reach each other through the internet when they're on the same LAN.

sections.title: General Requirements and Behavior
sections.content:
IPv6 Routing: The IPv6 CE router must implement IPv6 routing—looking up destination IPv6 addresses and forwarding packets to the right interface. It must comply with core IPv6 specifications and implement ICMP for diagnostics and error reporting.

Address Validation: Before forwarding any traffic between LAN and WAN, the router must complete IPv6 address acquisition on the WAN side. This prevents invalid routing during startup.

Router Advertisement Behavior: The router must include the Route Information Option in its router advertisements to announce the prefixes it has. It must not advertise itself as a default router if it has no prefixes assigned, preventing devices from using it when it has nothing to offer.

Weak Host Model: The router follows the weak host model where outgoing packets can use a source address from any of the router's interfaces, not just the outgoing one. This is necessary for routers that may need to originate packets using an address from an interface other than the one sending the packet.

Default Routing Behavior: By default, the router must not start dynamic routing protocols on its WAN interface. This keeps the network simple for most users, though advanced users can enable more complex setups.
sections.plainLanguage: The router forwards IPv6 packets correctly, doesn't send traffic out the wrong interface, and has sensible defaults so it works for typical home networks.

sections.title: Security Filtering and Protection
sections.content:
Ingress and Egress Filtering: The IPv6 CE router should support basic stateless filtering of obviously malicious traffic such as spoofed packets and invalid addresses (Martians). These filters prevent a compromised local device from spoofing addresses to attack external systems, and prevent external attackers from sending packets with fake source addresses into the local network.

Recommended Protections: The router should implement the security recommendations in RFC 6092, which includes filtering obviously malicious IPv6 traffic patterns. The router must support ingress filtering per BCP 38 to prevent IP source address spoofing attacks.

User-Configurable Filtering: While this document does not mandate specific mechanisms, the router should offer ways for users to configure packet filtering policies, though the implementation method is left to vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: The router filters out obviously fake or malicious packets, and prevents devices on your network from pretending to be something they're not.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 6204 is an Informational document that provided the definitive requirements for IPv6 customer edge routers as of April 2011. It was later obsoleted by RFC 7084, which provides updated requirements reflecting experience with IPv6 CE router deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo laid out the rules for IPv6 home routers in 2011. A newer RFC (7084) updated the rules later.
